items.body: Original asks students to "Comment on the authors' claim" (open-ended writing). MC conversion is the practical MOM choice, but instructors using this in a writing-emphasis context may want a companion essay prompt.
items.sug: No action needed unless a free-response variant is desired for a written assignment.

problems.original:
Possible randomized means. Data were collected on data from two groups (A and B). There were 3 measurements taken on Group A and two measurements in Group B.

\vspace{-2mm}

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

If the data are (repeatedly) randomly allocated across the two conditions, provide the following: (1) the values which are assigned to group A, (2) the values which are assigned to group B, and (3) the difference in averages $(\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B)$ for each of the following:

a. When the randomized difference in averages is as large as possible.

b. When the randomized difference in averages is as small as possible (a big in magnitude negative number).

c. When the randomized difference in averages is as close to zero as possible.

d. When the observed values are randomly assigned to the two groups, to which of the previous parts would you expect the difference in means to fall closest? Explain your reasoning.

items.body: The IMS original asks for three things per sub-part: (1) values assigned to Group A, (2) values assigned to Group B, and (3) the difference in averages. The MOM only asks for the difference, silently dropping parts (1) and (2). Students who get the right difference for the wrong allocation won't be caught.
items.sug: Add a second answer box per sub-part asking for the Group A values (e.g., as a sorted comma-separated list), or add a note that students should show their work in a scratch area.

problems.original:
Diamonds, mathematical test. We have data on two random samples of diamonds: one with diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and one with diamonds that weigh 1 carat. Each sample has 23 diamonds. Sample statistics for the price per carat of diamonds in each sample are provided below. Conduct a hypothesis test using a mathematical model to evaluate if there is a difference between the prices per carat of diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and diamonds that weigh 1 carat Make sure to state your hypotheses clearly, check relevant conditions, and interpret your results in context of the data. [@ggplot2]

\vspace{-3mm}

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

\vspace{-2mm}

items.body: The original asks students to state hypotheses, check conditions (independence, near-normality or n ≥ 30), and interpret results in context. The MOM reduces this to four numerical computations (SE, t, df, p-value), dropping condition-checking and interpretation.
items.sug: Add a fifth part as a multiple-choice "Conclusion" item (e.g., "Which of the following correctly interprets the result at α = 0.05?") to restore at least the interpretation step in auto-gradable form.

problems.original: A/B testing. A/B testing is a user experience research methodology where two variants of a page are shown to users at random. A company wants to evaluate whether users will spend more time, on average, on Page A or Page B using an A/B test. Two user experience designers at the company, Lucie and Müge, are tasked with conducting the analysis of the data collected. They agree on how the null hypothesis should be set: on average, users spend the same amount of time on Page A and Page B. Lucie believes that Page B will provide a better experience for users and hence wants to use a one-tailed test, Müge believes that a two-tailed test would be a better choice. Which designer do you agree with, and why?

items.body: The original is open-ended ("Which designer do you agree with, and why?") requiring students to construct a justification. The MC conversion captures the correct answer (Müge, two-tailed) but drops the reasoning component entirely.
items.sug: Accept as-is for auto-graded homework, but consider a companion free-response prompt for writing-emphasis contexts: "Explain in 1–2 sentences why a two-tailed test is more appropriate here."

problems.original:
Difference of means. We collect two random samples from two different populations In each part below, consider the sample means $\bar{x}_1$ and $\bar{x}_2$ that we might observe from these two samples.

\vspace{-1mm}

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

\vspace{-3mm}

a. What is the associated mean and standard deviation of $\bar{x}_1$?

b. What is the associated mean and standard deviation of $\bar{x}_2$?

c. Calculate and interpret the mean and standard deviation associated with the difference in sample means for the two groups, $\bar{x}_2 - \bar{x}_1$.

d. How are the standard deviations from parts (a), (b), and (c) related?

items.body: Part (d) of the original ("How are the standard deviations from parts (a), (b), and (c) related?") is dropped — the MOM covers only the six numerical answers for parts (a)–(c). Part (d) is a key conceptual payoff (SE_diff = √(SE₁² + SE₂²)) and the only part that asks students to articulate the relationship.
items.sug: Add a 7th multiple-choice part: "Which equation correctly relates the three standard deviations computed above?" with choices including `SE_diff = √(SE₁² + SE₂²)`, `SE_diff = SE₁ + SE₂`, `SE_diff = (SE₁ + SE₂)/2`, and `SE_diff = SE₁ × SE₂`.

problems.original:
Fuel efficiency in the city. Each year the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) releases fuel economy data on cars manufactured in that year. Below are summary statistics on fuel efficiency (in miles/gallon) from random samples of cars with manual and automatic transmissions manufactured in 2021. Do these data provide strong evidence of a difference between the average fuel efficiency of cars with manual and automatic transmissions in terms of their average city mileage? [@data:epa2021]

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

items.body: The original frames this as a full hypothesis test ("Do these data provide strong evidence of a difference…?") but the MOM covers only the three computational steps (SE, t, p-value) with no conclusion part. Students compute the numbers but are never asked to state a decision or interpret the result in context.
items.sug: Add a fourth MC part: "Based on your p-value and α = 0.05, what is the appropriate conclusion?" with choices along the lines of (A) Reject H₀; there is strong evidence of a difference in average city MPG between transmission types. (B) Fail to reject H₀; the data do not provide strong evidence of a difference. (C) Accept H₀; the two groups have the same mean. (D) Cannot determine without knowing the sample standard deviations.

problems.original: Gaming, distracted eating, and intake. A group of researchers who are interested in the possible effects of distracting stimuli during eating, such as an increase or decrease in the amount of food consumption, monitored food intake for a group of 44 patients who were randomized into two equal groups. The treatment group ate lunch while playing solitaire, and the control group ate lunch without any added distractions. Patients in the treatment group ate 52.1 grams of biscuits, with a standard deviation of 45.1 grams, and patients in the control group ate 27.1 grams of biscuits, with a standard deviation of 26.4 grams. Do these data provide convincing evidence that the average food intake (measured in amount of biscuits consumed) is different for the patients in the treatment group compared to the control group? Assume that conditions for conducting inference using mathematical models are satisfied. [@Oldham:2011]

items.body: The original asks one open question ("Do these data provide convincing evidence…?") which requires a conclusion/interpretation. The MOM covers only the three computational steps (SE, t, p-value) with no conclusion part.
items.sug: Add a fourth MC part: "Based on your p-value and α = 0.05, what is the appropriate conclusion?" with options such as (A) Reject H₀; there is convincing evidence that distracted eaters consume more biscuits on average. (B) Fail to reject H₀; the data do not provide convincing evidence of a difference. (C) Accept H₀; average intake is the same in both groups. (D) Cannot determine without knowing the population standard deviation.

items.body: Original part (a) ("Describe the distributions of weights…") requires reading the boxplot and histogram figures and is dropped in the MOM — the MOM starts at original part (b). The visual description task cannot be auto-graded, but students miss the distribution-inspection step that motivates checking normality/spread before the t-test.
items.sug: Accept drop as-is for auto-graded homework, or add a brief MC "Which statement best describes the weight distributions?" to restore some EDA before the test.

problems.original:
Gaming, distracted eating, and recall. A group of researchers who are interested in the possible effects of distracting stimuli during eating, such as an increase or decrease in the amount of food consumption, monitored food intake for a group of 44 patients who were randomized into two equal groups.
The 22 patients in the treatment group who ate their lunch while playing solitaire were asked to do a serial-order recall of the food lunch items they ate.
The average number of items recalled by the patients in this group was 4.
9, with a standard deviation of 1.8.
The average number of items recalled by the patients in the control group (no distraction) was 6.1, with a standard deviation of 1.8.
Do these data provide strong evidence that the average numbers of food items recalled by the patients in the treatment and control groups are different?
Assume that conditions for conducting inference using mathematical models are satisfied.
[@Oldham:2011]

The diamonds data used in this exercise can be found in the ggplot2 R package.

The lizard_run data used in this exercise can be found in the openintro R package.

The chickwts data used in this exercise can be found in the datasets R package.

The epa2021 data used in this exercise can be found in the openintro R package.

items.body: The original asks one overall question ("Do these data provide strong evidence that the average numbers of food items recalled are different?") requiring a conclusion/interpretation. The MOM covers only the three computational steps (SE, t, p-value) with no conclusion part.
items.sug: Add a fourth MC part: "Based on your p-value and α = 0.05, what is the appropriate conclusion?" with options such as (A) Reject H₀; there is strong evidence that distracted eaters recall fewer food items on average. (B) Fail to reject H₀; the data do not provide strong evidence of a difference in recall. (C) Accept H₀; average recall is the same in both groups. (D) Cannot determine without knowing the population standard deviations.

problems.original: Air quality. Air quality measurements were collected in a random sample of 25 country capitals in 2013, and then again in the same cities in 2014. We would like to use these data to compare average air quality between the two years. Should we use a paired or non-paired test? Explain your reasoning.

items.body: Original requires an open explanation ("Explain your reasoning"), but MOM converts to pure MC with no written response. `$showanswer` provides the explanation as post-answer feedback, but students never have to articulate it themselves.
items.sug: Add a short free-text essay box (low-stakes, manual grading or ungraded) asking students to explain their choice, or accept the MC-only simplification as deliberate for auto-grading.

problems.original:
High School and Beyond, randomization test. The National Center of Education Statistics conducted a survey of high school seniors, collecting test data on reading, writing, and several other subjects. Here we examine a simple random sample of 200 students from this survey.

Side-by-side box plots of reading and writing scores as well as a histogram of the differences in scores are shown below. Also provided below is a histogram of randomized averages of paired differences of scores (read - write), with the observed difference ($\bar{x}_{read-write} = -0.545$) marked with a red vertical line. The randomization distribution was produced by doing the following 1000 times: for each student, the two scores were randomly assigned to either read or write, and the average was taken across all students in the sample.

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

a. Is there a clear difference in the average reading and writing scores?

b. Are the reading and writing scores of each student independent of each other?

c. Create hypotheses appropriate for the following research question: is there an evident difference in the average scores of students in the reading and writing exam?

d. Is the average of the observed difference in scores $(\bar{x}_{read-write} = -0.545)$ consistent with the distribution of randomized average differences? Explain.

e. Do these data provide convincing evidence of a difference between the average scores on the two exams? Estimate the p-value from the randomization test, and conclude the hypothesis test using words like "score on reading test" and "score on writing test."

items.body: Converted to R-rendered seed-pool — verify the plot matches the question and the variants span sensible cases.

problems.original:
Global warming, randomization test. Let's consider a limited set of climate data, examining temperature differences in 1950 vs 2022. We sampled 26 locations in the US from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) historical data, where the data was available for both years of interest. [@webpage:noaa19482018] The data are not a random sample, but they are selected to be a representative sample across the land area of the lower 48 United States. Using the hottest day of the year as a measure can make the results susceptible to outliers. Instead, to get a sense for how hot a year was, we calculate the 90$^{th}$ percentile; that is, we find the maximum temperature on the day that was hotter than 90% of the days that year. We want to know: is the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature greater in 2022 or in 1950? The difference in 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature (high temperature for 2022 - high temperature for 1950) was calculated for each of the 26 locations. The average of the 26 differences was 2.52$^\circ$F with a standard deviation of 2.95$^\circ$F. We are interested in determining whether these data provide strong evidence that the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature is higher in 2022 than in 1950.

:::: {layout="[-0.05, 0.45, -0.05, 0.45]"} :::{#question} a. Create hypotheses appropriate for the following research question: is there an evident difference in the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temp across the two years (1950 and 2022)?\

b. Is the average of the observed difference in scores $(\bar{x}_{2022-1950} = 2.53$\^\circ$F)$ consistent with the distribution of randomized average differences? Explain. ::: :::{#plot} 📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab] ::: ::::

c. Do these data provide convincing evidence of a difference between the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature? Estimate the p-value from the randomization test, and conclude the hypothesis test using words like "90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature in 1950" and "90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature in 2022."

items.body: Parts (b) and (c) are entirely absent from the MOM. Part (b) asks whether the observed mean difference (2.53°F) is consistent with the randomization distribution (requires the histogram figure); part (c) asks students to estimate the p-value from that plot and draw a conclusion. Together they are the conceptual core of the exercise.
items.sug: Once the R-rendered randomization distribution figure is available, add parts (b) and (c) as free-response essay boxes (or add a figure-todo item to the figure pipeline pass).

problems.original:
High School and Beyond, bootstrap interval. We considered the differences between the reading and writing scores of a random sample of 200 students who took the High School and Beyond Survey. The mean and standard deviation of the differences are $\bar{x}{read-write} = -0.545$ and $s$ = 8.887 points. The bootstrap distribution below was produced by bootstrapping from the sample of differences in reading and writing scores 1,000 times.

:::: {layout="[-0.05, 0.45, -0.05, 0.45]"} :::{#question} a. Find an approximate 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the true average difference in scores (read - write).\

b. Find an approximate 95% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the true average difference in scores (read - write). ::: :::{#plot} 📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab] ::: ::::

c. Interpret both confidence intervals using words like "population" and "score".

d. From the confidence intervals calculated above, does it appear that there is a discernible difference in reading and writing scores, on average?

items.body: The MOM covers only part (b) of the original (bootstrap SE CI). Part (a) asks for a 95% bootstrap *percentile* CI by reading the bootstrap histogram — once the R-rendered figure is available this could be added as a read-the-plot question. Parts (c) and (d) are interpretation/conclusion questions (reasonable to omit for auto-grading, but the percentile-CI part is a meaningful gap).
items.sug: Add a figure-todo item for part (a) when the figure pipeline runs, or add a free-response essay box for the interpretation parts if desired.

problems.original:
Global warming, bootstrap interval. We considered the change in the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature in 1950 versus 2022 at 26 sampled locations from the NOAA database. [@webpage:noaa19482018] The mean and standard deviation of the reported differences are 2.53$^\circ$F and 2.95$^\circ$F.

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

a. Calculate a 90% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the average difference of 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature between 1950 and 2022.

b. Calculate a 90% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the average difference of 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature between 1950 and 2022.

c. Interpret both intervals in context.

d. Do the confidence intervals provide convincing evidence that there were hotter high temperatures in 2022 than in 1950 at NOAA stations? Explain your reasoning.

items.body: Part (a) — 90% bootstrap *percentile* CI — is dropped from the MOM. Reading the 5th and 95th percentiles off the 1,000-replicate bootstrap histogram (the R code block in ims-source) is the key skill being tested here and can't be computed from summary stats alone.
items.sug: Add a figure-todo item so the seed-pool (R-rendered) bootstrap histogram is available; once it is, restore part (a) as a read-the-plot pair of answer boxes (lower/upper percentile bounds).

items.body: Parts (c) and (d) — interpret both CIs in context; determine whether the CIs provide convincing evidence of warming — are absent. These mirror the same dropped parts in IMS 21.8 (same dataset/structure).
items.sug: Add free-response essay boxes for interpretation and conclusion, or add a MC part (d) on whether both CI bounds are positive → evidence of warming.

problems.original:
High School and Beyond, mathematical test. We considered the differences between the reading and writing scores of a random sample of 200 students who took the High School and Beyond Survey.

a. Create hypotheses appropriate for the following research question: is there an evident difference in the average scores of students in the reading and writing exam?

b. Check the conditions required to complete this test.

c. The average observed difference in scores is $\bar{x}{read-write} = -0.545$, and the standard deviation of the differences is $s = 8.887$ points. Do these data provide convincing evidence of a difference between the average scores on the two exams?

d. What type of error might we have made? Explain what the error means in the context of the application.

e. Based on the results of this hypothesis test, would you expect a confidence interval for the average difference between the reading and writing scores to include 0? Explain your reasoning.

\vfill

items.body: Original parts (a) and (b) — state hypotheses and check paired t-test conditions — are absent from the MOM. The MOM jumps straight to computation. Part (a) is straightforward MC (H₀: μ_diff = 0 vs. H_A: μ_diff ≠ 0).
items.sug: Add a MC part (a) presenting four hypothesis-pair options; add a MC or checklist part (b) covering the three conditions (random sample, independence, normality/n ≥ 30).

items.body: Original parts (d) and (e) — identify the possible error type in context, and reason about whether a CI would include 0 — are dropped. Both are highly MC-able given the randomized $decision variable already computed.
items.sug: Add MC part (e): "What type of error might have been made?" with options Type I / Type II / Cannot determine, keyed to `$errortype`. Add MC part (f): "Based on your p-value, would a 95% CI for the mean difference include 0?" keyed to whether `$pval >= $alpha_val`.

problems.original:
High school and beyond, mathematical interval. We considered the differences between the reading and writing scores of a random sample of 200 students who took the High School and Beyond Survey. The mean and standard deviation of the differences are $\bar{x}{read-write} = -0.545$ and $s$ = 8.887 points.

a. Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the average difference between the reading and writing scores of all students.

b. Interpret this interval in context.

c. Does the confidence interval provide convincing evidence that there is a real difference in the average scores? Explain.

items.body: Original parts (b) and (c) are absent. Part (b) asks students to interpret the confidence interval in context; part (c) asks whether the CI provides convincing evidence of a real difference between reading and writing scores (i.e., does the interval exclude 0?). Both are auto-gradable: part (c) is a MC keyed to whether `$lower > 0` or `$upper < 0` (interval excludes 0 → convincing evidence); part (b) could be a fill-in-the-blanks sentence using `$lower`, `$upper`, and `$context`.
items.sug: Add MC part (g): "Based on your CI, is there convincing evidence of a real average difference?" keyed to `($upper < 0 || $lower > 0)`.

problems.original:
Global warming, mathematical interval. We considered the change in the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature in 1950 versus 2022 at 26 sampled locations from the NOAA database. [@webpage:noaa19482018] The mean and standard deviation of the reported differences are 2.53$^\circ$F and 2.95$^\circ$F.

a. Calculate a 90% confidence interval for the average difference of 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature between 1950 and 2022. We've already checked the conditions for you.

b. Interpret the interval in context.

c. Does the confidence interval provide convincing evidence that there were hotter high temperatures in 2022 than in 1950 at NOAA stations? Explain your reasoning.

items.body: Original parts (b) and (c) are dropped. Part (b) asks students to interpret the 90% CI in context (what does the interval say about the change in 90th-percentile high temperatures?); part (c) asks whether the CI provides convincing evidence that 2022 temperatures were higher than 1950 (i.e., does the entire interval lie above 0?). Part (c) is straightforwardly auto-gradable: key to `($lower > 0)`.
items.sug: Add MC part (f): "Does your CI provide convincing evidence that 90th-percentile high temperatures were higher in 2022 than in 1950?" with options Yes/No keyed to `($lower > 0) ? "Yes" : "No"`. Part (b) interpretation could be a fill-in-the-blank sentence or a free-response essay box.

items.body: Original parts (a), (b), (c), (f), and (g) are all absent from the MOM. Part (a) asks whether the 1950/2022 observations are paired or independent (conceptual MC); part (b) asks students to write the hypotheses in symbols and words; part (c) asks whether the paired t-test conditions are met (given the histogram of differences); part (f) asks which error type might have occurred given the decision; part (g) asks whether a CI for the mean difference would include 0 and why. The MOM covers only the computation steps (SE, t, df, p-value, decision).
items.sug: Add MC part for hypotheses (H₀: μ_diff = 0 vs. H_A: μ_diff ≠ 0) and a MC part for error type keyed to `$decision` (Type I if reject H₀, Type II if fail to reject); optionally add a MC part (g) on whether the CI includes 0 keyed to `($pval >= $alpha_val)`. Parts (a) and (c) require free-response or the difference histogram figure.

problems.original:
Study environment. In order to test the effects of listening to music while studying versus studying in silence, students agree to be randomized to two treatments (i.e., study with music or study in silence). There are two exams during the semester, so the researchers can either randomize the students to have one exam with music and one with silence (randomly selecting which exam corresponds to which study environment) or the researchers can randomize the students to one study habit for both exams.

The researchers are interested in estimating the true population difference of exam score for those who listen to music while studying as compared to those who study in silence.

a. Describe the experiment which is consistent with a paired designed experiment. How is the treatment assigned, and how are the data collected such that the observations are paired?

b. Describe the experiment which is consistent with an indpenedent samples experiment. How is the treatment assigned, and how are the data collected such that the observations are independent?

items.body: The original asks students to *describe* in their own words what makes each design paired vs. independent (open response). The MOM converts both parts to recognition MC (pick the correct description from a list). The generative articulation skill is lost.
items.sug: Accept the MC simplification as deliberate for auto-grading, or add a short free-response essay box asking students to explain why one design produces paired observations and the other does not.

items.body: Both parts (a) and (b) draw from the same 4-choice pool. Once a student correctly picks the paired design for part (a), the independent-samples answer for part (b) becomes nearly obvious by elimination, making the second part trivially easy.
items.sug: Either use disjoint choice pools for each part, or combine into a single question ("Match each design to its type") to avoid the give-away structure.

problems.original:
Friday the 13th, traffic. In the early 1990's, researchers in the UK collected data on traffic flow on Friday the 13th with the goal of addressing issues of how superstitions regarding Friday the 13th affect human behavior and and whether Friday the 13th is an unlucky day. The histograms below show the distributions of numbers of cars passing by a specific intersection on Friday the 6th and Friday the 13th for many such date pairs. Also provided are some sample statistics, where the difference is the number of cars on the 6th minus the number of cars on the 13th. [@Scanlon:1993]

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

a. Are there any underlying structures in these data that should be considered in an analysis? Explain.

b. What are the hypotheses for evaluating whether the number of people out on Friday the 6$^{\text{th}}$ is different than the number out on Friday the 13$^{\text{th}}$?

c. Check conditions to carry out the hypothesis test from part (b) using mathematical models.

d. Calculate the test statistic and the p-value.

e. What is the conclusion of the hypothesis test?

f. Interpret the p-value in this context.

g. What type of error might have been made in the conclusion of your test? Explain.

\vfill

items.body: The Friday the 13th traffic context (Scanlon 1993 UK study) is entirely absent from the question text; it only says "Researchers collected paired measurements on $n date pairs." The randomized parameters ($dbar ∈ [−5, 5], $sd ∈ [2, 6]) also bear no resemblance to the original data scale (mean difference ≈ 1,836 cars, SD ≈ 1,176 cars).
items.sug: Restore the concrete scenario in the question text ("In a UK study of Friday the 13th superstitions, researchers recorded traffic counts at the same intersection on Friday the 6th and Friday the 13th for $n paired dates…") and adjust the randomization ranges to plausible car-count differences (e.g., $dbar ∈ [500, 3000], $sd ∈ [500, 2000]).

items.body: Original parts (a), (b), (c), and (f) are absent. Part (a) asks whether there are underlying structures in the data (paired design — the same locations observed on two days); part (b) asks students to state the hypotheses; part (c) asks them to check paired t-test conditions using the provided histograms; part (f) asks them to interpret the p-value in context (not just state the decision). The MOM covers only the computation steps and the error-type conclusion.
items.sug: Add MC part for hypotheses (H₀: μ_diff = 0 vs. H_A: μ_diff ≠ 0); add MC part for the paired-design rationale (same location/day pairs → paired structure); add MC part for p-value interpretation keyed to whether $pval < $alpha_val and the direction of $dbar. Parts (b) and (c) that depend on histograms would require the figure pipeline.

problems.original:
Friday the 13th, accidents. In the early 1990's, researchers in the UK collected data the number of traffic accident related emergency room (ER) admissions on Friday the 13th with the goal of addressing issues of how superstitions regarding Friday the 13th affect human behavior and and whether Friday the 13th is an unlucky day. The histograms below show the distributions of numbers of ER admissions at specific emergency rooms on Friday the 6th and Friday the 13th for many such date pairs. Also provided are some sample statistics, where the difference is the ER admissions on the 6th minus the ER admissions on the 13th.[@Scanlon:1993]

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

a. Conduct a hypothesis test using mathematical models to evaluate if there is a difference between the average numbers of traffic accident related emergency room admissions between Friday the 6$^{\text{th}}$ and Friday the 13$^{\text{th}}$.

b. Calculate a 95% confidence interval using mathematical models for the difference between the average numbers of traffic accident related emergency room admissions between Friday the 6$^{\text{th}}$ and Friday the 13$^{\text{th}}$.

c. The conclusion of the original study states, "Friday 13th is unlucky for some. The risk of hospital admission as a result of a transport accident may be increased by as much as 52%. Staying at home is recommended." Do you agree with this statement? Explain your reasoning.

\vspace{10mm}

items.body: Original part (c) — students evaluate the study's dramatic conclusion ("Friday 13th is unlucky for some. The risk of hospital admission as a result of a transport accident may be increased by as much as 52%. Staying at home is recommended.") and explain whether they agree — is absent from the MOM. This is the interpretive payoff of the exercise.
items.sug: Add a MC part (c) presenting 3–4 interpretive stances (e.g., "Yes, the data strongly support the 52% claim"; "The test shows a significant difference but doesn't directly estimate a 52% increase in risk"; "No, the p-value was not significant so the conclusion is unjustified") keyed to the randomized $pval and $dbar to ensure the correct answer matches the computed result.

problems.original: Fill in the blank. When doing an ANOVA, you observe large differences in means between groups. Within the ANOVA framework, this would most likely be interpreted as evidence strongly favoring the _____________ hypothesis.

items.body: String fill-in answer "alternative" will get `$anstypes="number"` from deploy.py, which is wrong for a word — convert to multiple-choice with options: alternative / null / two-sided / one-sided.
items.sug: Replace `$answerbox[0]` fill-in with a radio question; `$answer[0] = 0`; `$choices_a = array("alternative","null","two-sided","one-sided")`.

problems.original: Which test? We would like to test if students who are in the social sciences, natural sciences, arts and humanities, and other fields spend the same amount of time, on average, studying for a course. What type of test should we use? Explain your reasoning.

items.body: Original asks students to "explain your reasoning" (open response), but .mom converts it to a radio MC — students just pick ANOVA with no justification.
items.sug: Add a short free-response follow-up (second answer box) asking why ANOVA is appropriate, or accept the MC-only version if conceptual recall is sufficient for this course.

items.body: `$pval = round(fcdf($F_stat, $df_b, $df_w), 4)` computes the *lower* tail CDF, not the upper-tail p-value. A large F (e.g. 3.8, df 2/197) gives pval ≈ 0.976 > 0.05, so the conclusion flips to "Fail to reject" when it should be "Reject."
items.sug: Replace with `$pval = round(1 - fcdf($F_stat, $df_b, $df_w), 4)` (upper tail).

problems.original:
Beer and blood alcohol content. Many people believe that weight, drinking habits, and many other factors are much more important in predicting blood alcohol content (BAC) than simply considering the number of drinks a person consumed. Here we examine data from sixteen student volunteers at Ohio State University who each drank a randomly assigned number of cans of beer. These students were evenly divided between men and women, and they differed in weight and drinking habits. Thirty minutes later, a police officer measured their blood alcohol content (BAC) in grams of alcohol per deciliter of blood. The scatterplot and regression table summarize the findings. [@Malkevitc+Lesser:2008]

📊 [original figure — see Rendered tab]

a. Describe the relationship between the number of cans of beer and BAC.

b. Write the equation of the regression line. Interpret the slope and intercept in context.

d. The correlation coefficient for number of cans of beer and BAC is r r_bac. Calculate $R^2$ and interpret it in context.
